title: The Further Adventures of Toad
paragraphs: The front door of the hollow tree faced east, so Toad got his wake-up call early. It came partly from the bright sunlight pouring in on him, and partly from the terrible chill in his toes, which made him dream that he was at home in bed in his own fine room with the Tudor window, on a freezing winter night. In the dream his blankets had gotten up, grumbling and complaining that they couldn’t stand the cold one minute longer, and had run downstairs to warm themselves at the kitchen fire. He had followed them in his bare feet, along miles and miles of icy stone passages, arguing with them and begging them to be reasonable. He would probably have woken much sooner if he hadn’t spent weeks sleeping on straw over stone floors, and nearly forgotten how friendly thick blankets feel when they’re pulled up snugly under your chin.

He sat up and rubbed his eyes, then his complaining toes. For a moment he wondered where he was, and looked around for the familiar stone wall and the little barred window. Then, with a jump of his heart, he remembered everything: his escape, his flight, his pursuit. He remembered, first and best of all, that he was free!

Free! That one word and the thought behind it were worth fifty blankets. He felt warm from head to toe as he thought about the jolly world outside, which was surely waiting eagerly for his grand and triumphant entrance, ready to wait on him and cheer him on, anxious to help him and keep him company, just as it had always done in the old days before misfortune struck. He shook himself and combed the dry leaves out of his hair with his fingers. Then, his washing and dressing done, he marched out into the pleasant morning sun, cold but confident, hungry but hopeful, with all the nervous terrors of yesterday swept away by rest and sleep and honest, heartening sunshine.

He had the whole world to himself that early summer morning. The dewy woods, as he made his way through them, were empty and still. The green fields beyond the trees were his to do with as he liked. And the road itself, when he reached it, seemed in all that loneliness to be looking anxiously for company, like a stray dog. Toad, however, was looking for something that could talk and tell him plainly which way to go. It is all very well, when you have a light heart, a clear conscience and money in your pocket, and nobody combing the countryside to haul you back to prison, to follow wherever the road beckons and points, without caring where it leads. The practical Toad cared very much indeed, and he could have kicked the road for its helpless silence, when every minute counted.

Before long the shy, silent country road was joined by a bashful little brother in the form of a canal, which took its hand and wandered along beside it in perfect trust, though it had the same tongue-tied, close-mouthed manner toward strangers. “Bother them!” Toad said to himself. “But anyhow, one thing’s clear. They must both be coming _from_ somewhere, and going _to_ somewhere. You can’t argue with that. Toad, my boy!” So he marched patiently on along the water’s edge.

Around a bend in the canal came a lone horse, plodding along with his head bent as if lost in worried thought. A long line ran from the ropes on his collar, tight but sagging a little with each step, and the far end of it dripped pearly drops of water. Toad let the horse go by and stood waiting to see what the fates were sending him.

With a pleasant swirl of quiet water at its blunt bow, the barge slid up beside him. Its cheerfully painted side was level with the towpath, and its only occupant was a big, stout woman in a linen sun-bonnet, one brawny arm resting along the tiller.
“Lovely morning, ma’am!” she called to Toad as she came level with him.

“I dare say it is, ma’am!” Toad answered politely, walking along the towpath beside her. “I dare say it _is_ a lovely morning for those who aren’t in serious trouble, like I am. Here’s my married daughter, who sends for me in a great hurry to come to her right away. So off I go, not knowing what’s happening or about to happen, but fearing the worst, as you’ll understand, ma’am, if you’re a mother too. And I’ve left my business to look after itself—I’m in the washing and laundry line, you must know, ma’am—and I’ve left my little children to look after themselves, and a more mischievous and troublesome set of young imps never lived, ma’am! And I’ve lost all my money, and lost my way, and as for what may be happening to my married daughter, well, I can’t bear to think of it, ma’am!”
“And where does your married daughter live, ma’am?” asked the barge-woman.
“She lives near the river, ma’am,” said Toad. “Close to a fine house called Toad Hall, somewhere around here, in these parts. Perhaps you’ve heard of it.”

“Toad Hall? Why, I’m headed that way myself,” said the barge-woman. “This canal meets the river a few miles on, just above Toad Hall, and from there it’s an easy walk. Come along on the barge with me, and I’ll give you a ride.”

She steered the barge in close to the bank, and Toad, with many humble and grateful thanks, stepped lightly aboard and sat down, extremely pleased with himself. “Toad’s luck again!” he thought. “I always land on top!”
“So you’re in the washing business, ma’am?” the barge-woman said politely as they glided along. “And a very good business it is, I’m sure, if I’m not being too bold in saying so.”

“The finest business in the whole country,” Toad said breezily. “All the gentry come to me. They wouldn’t go to anyone else, not if you paid them, they know me so well. You see, I understand my trade inside out, and I look after everything myself. Washing, ironing, starching, fine shirts for gentlemen’s evening wear—all of it is done right under my own eye!”
“Surely you don’t do _all_ that work with your own two hands, ma’am?” the barge-woman asked, with respect in her voice.
“Oh, I have girls,” Toad said airily. “Twenty or so, always hard at work. But you know what _girls_ are like, ma’am! Nasty little hussies, that’s what _I_ call them!”
“So do I,” said the barge-woman heartily. “But I expect you keep yours in line, the lazy good-for-nothings! And are you _very_ fond of washing?”

“Love it?” said Toad. “I’m simply mad about it. Nothing makes me happier than standing with both arms plunged in the suds. But then, I have such a knack for it! There’s no effort in it whatsoever! Pure delight, ma’am, I promise you!”
“What a stroke of luck, running into you!” the barge-woman remarked thoughtfully. “A real bit of good fortune for the both of us!”
“Why, what do you mean?” asked Toad nervously.

“Well, look at me,” said the barge-woman. “_I_ like washing too, just as you do. And whether I like it or not, I have to do all my own, naturally, moving around the way I do. Now my husband is such a one for dodging his work and leaving the barge to me that I never get a moment to see to my own business. By rights he ought to be here now, either steering or looking after the horse, though luckily the horse has the sense to look after himself. Instead of which, he’s gone off with the dog to see if they can’t catch a rabbit for dinner somewhere. Says he’ll catch up with me at the next lock. Well, we’ll see about that. I don’t trust him once he’s off with that dog, who’s even worse than he is. But in the meantime, how am I supposed to get on with my washing?”
“Oh, never mind the washing,” said Toad, who didn’t like the subject. “Try to keep your mind on that rabbit. A nice fat young rabbit, I’ll bet. Have you got any onions?”

“I can’t think about anything but my washing,” said the barge-woman, “and I’m amazed you can go on about rabbits with such a happy prospect ahead of you. I’ve got a whole heap of things stacked in a corner of the cabin. Just pick out one or two of the most necessary kind—I won’t embarrass a lady like you by describing them, but you’ll know them at a glance—and run them through the wash-tub as we go along. Why, it’ll be a pleasure for you, as you say yourself, and a real help to me. You’ll find a tub handy, plus soap, a kettle on the stove, and a bucket for hauling water up from the canal. Then I’ll know you’re enjoying yourself, rather than sitting around idle, gazing at the scenery and yawning your head off.”

“Here, let me do the steering!” said Toad, now thoroughly scared. “Then you can do your washing however you like. I might ruin your things, or not do them the way you want. I’m used to gentlemen’s clothes, really. That’s my specialty.”

“You, steer?” the barge-woman said with a laugh. “Steering a barge well takes a good deal of practice. And anyway, it’s boring work, and I’d like to see you enjoying yourself. No, you’ll get on with the washing you’re so crazy about, and I’ll keep to the tiller, which I know. Please don’t cheat me out of the joy of treating you!”

Toad was well and truly trapped. He looked this way and that for a way out, saw he was too far from the bank to jump, and sulkily gave in to his fate. “If it comes to that,” he thought desperately, “I suppose any fool can _wash!_”
He fetched a tub, soap and the other necessities from the cabin, picked out a few garments at random, tried to remember what he had seen in quick glances through laundry windows, and set to work.

Half an hour dragged by, and with each minute Toad grew more furious. Nothing he did to those wretched things seemed to please them or improve them in the slightest. He coaxed them, he slapped them, he pounded them with his fists; and all the while they grinned up at him from the tub, quite unreformed and perfectly happy in their original sin. Now and then he shot a nervous glance over his shoulder at the barge-woman, but she seemed to be staring off ahead, wholly taken up with her steering. His back hurt terribly, and to his horror he saw that his paws were starting to go all puckered. And Toad was extremely vain about his paws. Under his breath he mumbled words that no washerwoman and no Toad should ever let slip; and for the fiftieth time, the soap got away from him.
A sudden roar of laughter made him pull himself upright and spin around. There sat the barge-woman, thrown back in her seat, laughing helplessly, with tears streaming down her cheeks.

“I’ve been watching you the whole time,” she gasped. “I guessed you must be a fraud from the start, from the stuck-up way you talked. Some washerwoman you are! You never washed so much as a dishcloth in your life, I’ll bet!”
For quite a while Toad’s temper had been seething away nastily, and now it boiled right over. He lost all hold on himself.

“You common, vulgar, _fat_ barge-woman!” he bellowed. “How dare you speak to your betters in that tone! Washerwoman, indeed! Let me inform you that I am a Toad, a famous, respected, distinguished Toad! Things may look a little cloudy for me just now, but I refuse, absolutely _refuse_, to be laughed at by a barge-woman!”

The woman stepped closer and bent down to squint sharply under his bonnet. “Well, so you are!” she exclaimed. “I never did! A horrible, nasty, creeping Toad! And on my own clean barge, too! I won’t stand for _that_, and that’s flat.”

Letting go of the tiller for an instant, she flung out one huge, speckled arm and seized Toad by a front leg; her other hand clamped hard around a hind leg. Next, the whole world flipped upside down, the barge seemed to float lightly away across the sky, the wind shrieked past his ears, and Toad was sailing through the air, turning over and over as he flew.

The water, when he finally reached it with a loud splash, turned out to be quite cold enough for his taste, though its chill wasn’t enough to quench his proud spirit or cool the heat of his furious temper. He came up spluttering, and when he had wiped the duckweed out of his eyes, the first thing he saw was the fat barge-woman looking back at him over the stern of the departing barge and laughing. As he coughed and choked, he vowed to get even with her.

He struck out for the shore, but the cotton gown got badly in his way, and when he finally touched land he found it hard to climb the steep bank without help. He had to rest a minute or two to catch his breath. Then, gathering his wet skirts up over his arms, he started running after the barge as fast as his legs would carry him, wild with indignation and thirsting for revenge.

The barge-woman was still laughing as he came running up alongside. “Feed yourself through the mangle, washerwoman,” she called, “then iron your face flat and give it a crimp, and you’ll make a perfectly respectable-looking Toad!”

Toad didn’t bother to answer. What he craved was solid revenge, not cheap, breezy triumphs made of words, although he had one or two remarks tucked away that he would happily have delivered. Instead, he spotted just what he needed up ahead. He dashed forward and caught up with the horse, slipped the towrope loose and let it fall, sprang lightly onto the horse’s back, and drove it into a gallop with some hearty kicks in the ribs. Leaving the towpath behind, he turned his mount toward open country and down a bumpy lane. Once he glanced back: the barge had run aground against the opposite bank of the canal, and the barge-woman was flinging her arms about and yelling, “Stop, stop, stop!” “I’ve heard that tune before,” said Toad with a laugh, and he spurred his steed on through its headlong race.

The barge-horse wasn’t built for any very long effort, and its gallop soon slowed to a trot, and its trot to an easy walk. But Toad was perfectly content with this, knowing that he, at any rate, was moving, and the barge was not. He had quite recovered his temper now that he had done something he considered really clever. He was happy to jog along quietly in the sun, steering his horse along side roads and bridle-paths, and trying to forget how very long it had been since his last square meal, until the canal was left far behind him.

He had traveled some miles, his horse and he, and he was feeling drowsy in the hot sunshine, when the horse stopped, lowered his head and began to nibble the grass. Toad woke up and only just saved himself from tumbling off, with an effort. He looked around and found that he was on a wide common, dotted as far as he could see with patches of gorse and bramble. Near him stood a shabby gypsy caravan, and beside it a man sat on an upturned bucket, very busy smoking and staring out at the wide world. A fire of sticks was burning close by, and over the fire hung an iron pot, and out of that pot came bubblings and gurglings and a vague, suggestive steaminess. There were smells, too—warm, rich and varied smells—that twined and twisted and wreathed themselves at last into one complete, luscious, perfect smell, which seemed like the very soul of Nature taking shape and appearing to her children, a true Goddess, a mother of solace and comfort. Toad now knew very well that he had not really been hungry before. What he had felt earlier in the day had been a mere trifling pang. This was the real thing at last, no mistake about it, and it would have to be dealt with quickly, or there would be trouble for somebody or something. He looked the gypsy over carefully, wondering vaguely whether it would be easier to fight him or to sweet-talk him. So there he sat, sniffing and sniffing and looking at the gypsy, and the gypsy sat and smoked, and looked at him.
After a while the gypsy took the pipe out of his mouth and asked, as if it hardly mattered, “Want to sell that horse of yours?”

Toad was completely caught off guard. He had no idea that gypsies loved a bit of horse-trading and never passed up a chance at it, and it hadn’t crossed his mind that caravans were always traveling and needed a lot of pulling. He had never thought of turning the horse into cash, but the gypsy’s question seemed to open a path toward the two things he wanted so badly—ready money and a hearty breakfast.

“What?” he said. “Me, sell this beautiful young horse of mine? Oh, no; that’s out of the question. Who would take the laundry home to my customers every week? Besides, I’m far too fond of him, and he simply adores me.”
“Try loving a donkey instead,” suggested the gypsy. “Some folks do.”

“Apparently it escapes you,” Toad went on, “that this splendid horse of mine is far above your station. He’s partly a blood horse, you see; not the part that shows, naturally—some other part. And in his time he won prizes as a Hackney, too—that was before your day, mind you, but anybody who knows a thing about horses can still spot it right away. No, no, selling him is not to be thought of for a moment. Still, what would you care to offer me for this beautiful young horse of mine?”

The gypsy looked the horse over, then looked Toad over just as carefully, then looked at the horse again. “A shilling a leg,” he said shortly, and turned away, puffing on his pipe and staring down the whole wide world.
“A shilling a leg?” cried Toad. “Kindly give me a little time to figure that out and see exactly what it adds up to.”

He climbed down from his horse, left it to graze, sat down beside the gypsy, and counted on his fingers. At last he said, “A shilling a leg? Why, that comes to exactly four shillings, and not a penny more. Oh, no; I couldn’t dream of taking four shillings for this beautiful young horse of mine.”
“Well,” said the gypsy, “I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I’ll make it five shillings, and that’s three and sixpence more than the animal is worth. And that’s my final word.”

Then Toad sat and thought it over, long and hard. He was hungry and had no money at all, he was still some distance from home—he couldn’t tell how far—and his enemies might still be hunting for him. To someone in that position, five shillings can look like a great deal of money. On the other hand, it didn’t seem like much to get for a horse. But then again, the horse hadn’t cost him a thing, so whatever he got was pure profit. At last he said firmly, “Listen here, gypsy! I’ll tell you what we’ll do; and this is _my_ final word. You will hand over six shillings and sixpence, cash on the spot; and in addition to that, you will give me as much breakfast as I can possibly eat, at one sitting of course, out of that iron pot of yours that keeps sending out such delicious, exciting smells. In return, I will hand over my spirited young horse, with all the beautiful harness and trimmings on him thrown in for free. If that’s not good enough for you, say so, and I’ll be on my way. I know a man near here who’s wanted this horse of mine for years.”

The gypsy grumbled terribly and declared that a few more deals like this would ruin him. But in the end he dragged a grubby canvas bag from deep in his trouser pocket and counted six shillings and sixpence into Toad’s paw. Then he ducked into the caravan for a moment and came back with a big iron plate and a knife, fork, and spoon. He tipped up the pot, and a glorious stream of hot, rich stew gurgled onto the plate. It was truly the most beautiful stew in the world, made of partridges, and pheasants, and chickens, and hares, and rabbits, and peahens, and guinea fowl, and one or two other things. Toad held the plate on his lap, nearly in tears, and ate, and ate, and ate, and kept asking for more, and the gypsy never begrudged him any. He thought he had never had so good a breakfast in all his life.

Once Toad had loaded up on as much stew as he believed he could hold, he stood, told the gypsy good-bye, and bade the horse a tender farewell. The gypsy knew the riverside well and pointed out the way, and off Toad went on his travels again, in the highest of spirits. He was really a very different Toad from the creature he had been an hour earlier. The sun was shining brightly, his damp clothes had dried out completely, there was money in his pocket again, home and friends and safety were drawing near, and best of all, he had put away a hearty, hot, filling meal, which left him feeling large and strong and carefree and full of himself.

Strolling along merrily, he went over his adventures and narrow escapes in his mind, and how, just when the situation looked blackest, he had always found his way out; and his pride and vanity started swelling up inside him. “Ho, ho!” he told himself as he marched on, chin held high, “how clever I am! There can’t be another animal anywhere as brilliant as Toad! My enemies locked me in a prison, ringed round with sentries and watched all day and all night by jailers; yet I simply stroll out past every one of them, thanks to my talent and my courage. They hunt me down with engines, and policemen, and revolvers; I snap my fingers in their faces and disappear, laughing, into thin air. Then, sadly, a woman with a fat body and a wicked mind tosses me into a canal. So what? I swim to the bank, I grab her horse, I gallop away in triumph, and I sell that horse for a pocketful of money and a splendid breakfast! Ho, ho! I am The Toad, the handsome, the popular, the successful Toad!” He swelled up so much with conceit that, as he walked, he composed a song praising himself and bellowed it at the top of his lungs, even though nobody was there to listen but Toad. Quite possibly it was the most boastful song any animal has ever written.

“The world has known great Heroes,
As history books have showed;
But none whose name will rise to fame
As high as that of Toad!

“The clever men at Oxford
Know all that there is to be knowed.
But not one of them knows half as much
As brilliant Mr. Toad!

“The animals sat in the Ark and wept,
Their tears in rivers flowed.
Who called out, ‘There’s land ahead!’?
The cheering Mr. Toad!

“The soldiers saluted smartly
As they marched down the road.
Was it the King? Or Kitchener?
Oh no—it was Mr. Toad.

“The Queen and her ladies-in-waiting
Sat at the window and sewed.
She cried, ‘Look! Who’s that _handsome_ man?’
They answered, ‘Mr. Toad.’”
The song went on for a great many more verses just like these, but they were far too vain to set down on paper. What you have here are some of the gentler ones.
He sang as he walked, and walked as he sang, and grew more puffed up with every minute. But his pride was about to take a nasty fall.

Several miles of country lanes later, he came out onto the high road. As he turned along it and gazed down its pale length, he spotted something heading his way: first a speck, then a dot, then a blob, and then something that looked very familiar indeed; and a double blast of warning, all too well known to him, reached his delighted ears.

“Now this is more like it!” said the excited Toad. “This is real life again, this is the great world once more, the world I’ve been missing for so long! I’ll hail them, my brothers of the wheel, and spin them a yarn, the kind that’s worked so well so far; and of course they’ll give me a lift, and then I’ll talk to them some more; and perhaps, with luck, it may even end with my driving up to Toad Hall in a motor-car! That will be a slap in the face for Badger!”

He strode confidently out into the road to flag down the motor-car, which was rolling along at an easy pace and slowing as it came up to the lane. Then all at once he went deathly pale, his heart melted into water, his knees shook and buckled under him, and he folded up and collapsed with a sickening pain in his stomach. And no wonder, the unhappy animal. For the car coming toward him was the very one he had stolen from the yard of the Red Lion Hotel on that fatal day when all his troubles began! And the people inside were the very same people he had sat watching at lunch in the coffee-room!

He sank into a shabby, wretched heap in the road, muttering in despair, “It’s all up! It’s all finished! Chains and policemen once more! Back to prison! Back to dry bread and water! Oh, what a fool I’ve been! Why did I have to go strutting around the countryside, singing conceited songs and flagging down strangers in broad daylight on the high road, when I could have hidden till dark and crept home quietly by the back ways! Oh, hapless Toad! Oh, ill-fated animal!”

The terrible motor-car crept nearer and nearer, until at last he heard it stop just short of him. Two gentlemen got out and walked around the trembling heap of crumpled misery lying in the road, and one of them said, “Oh dear! This is very sad! Here is a poor old soul—a washerwoman, it seems—who has fainted in the road! Perhaps the heat has overcome her, poor creature; or maybe she has had nothing to eat today. Let’s lift her into the car and take her to the nearest village, where no doubt she has friends.”
They gently lifted Toad into the motor-car, propped him up with soft cushions, and drove on.
When Toad heard them speaking so kindly and sympathetically, and realized that he hadn’t been recognized, his courage began to return, and he cautiously opened first one eye and then the other.
“Look,” said one of the gentlemen, “she’s already improving. It’s the fresh air that’s helping her. And how are you feeling now, ma’am?”
“Thank you so much, sir,” said Toad in a faint voice. “I feel ever so much better!” “Splendid,” said the gentleman. “Just lie perfectly still now, and most of all, don’t try to speak.”
“I won’t,” said Toad. “It’s only that I was thinking I’d be right as rain in no time if I could sit up front beside the driver, with the fresh air blowing straight into my face.”
“What a sensible woman!” said the gentleman. “Of course you may.” And so they carefully helped Toad up into the front seat next to the driver, and on they rolled.

Toad was almost himself again by now. He sat up and looked around, and tried to fight down the shivers, the yearnings, the old cravings that rose up and swarmed over him and took complete possession of him.
“Fate!” he told himself. “Why bother to strive? Why bother to struggle?” With that he turned to the driver beside him.

“Please, sir,” he said, “would you be so very kind as to let me have a go at driving the car for a bit? I’ve been watching you closely, and it seems so simple and so fascinating, and I would dearly love to tell my friends that I had once driven a motor-car!”

The driver found the request so funny that he roared with laughter, and the gentleman asked what was going on. When he was told, he said, to Toad’s great joy, “Bravo, ma’am! I admire your pluck. Give her a turn, and keep a close watch on her. She can’t do any harm.”

Toad eagerly scrambled into the seat the driver had left, took the steering wheel in his hands, listened with put-on humility to the instructions he was given, and set the car moving, but very slowly and carefully at first, for he was determined to be sensible.
The gentlemen in the back clapped their hands and cheered, and Toad heard them say, “How well she does it! Imagine a washerwoman driving as well as that, on her very first try!”
Toad went a little faster; then faster still, and faster.
The gentlemen shouted a warning from behind: “Careful there, washerwoman!” That irritated him, and he began to lose his head.

The driver made a move to take over, but Toad held him down in his seat with one elbow and opened the engine up all the way. The wind rushing at his face, the humming of the motor, and the light leaping of the car under him made his feeble brain reel as if he were drunk. “Washerwoman, indeed!” he cried wildly. “Ho! Ho! Behold the Toad, the motor-car snatcher, the jailbreaker, the Toad who always gets away! Sit tight and I’ll show you what driving truly is, because you’re being driven by the famous, the skillful, the absolutely fearless Toad!”

With a cry of horror, everyone in the car jumped up and hurled themselves at him. “Grab him!” they shouted. “Grab the Toad, the wicked animal who stole our motor-car! Tie him up, chain him, haul him to the nearest police station! Down with the desperate, dangerous Toad!”

Alas! They should have thought; they should have been more careful; they should have remembered to stop the motor-car somehow before trying any tricks like that. With a half-turn of the wheel, Toad sent the car crashing through the low hedge that ran along the roadside. One mighty leap, a violent jolt, and the wheels of the car were churning through the thick mud of a horse pond.

Suddenly Toad was soaring through the air, rising with the powerful lift and gentle arc of a swallow. He enjoyed it, and was just starting to wonder if he would keep on going until he sprouted wings and became a Toad-bird, when he came down flat on his back, with a thud, in the soft, lush grass of a meadow. He sat up. There, in the pond, was the motor-car, almost completely under water, and the gentlemen and the driver, hampered by their heavy long coats, were thrashing around in the water, quite unable to help themselves.

Quickly getting to his feet, he took off across the countryside at top speed, crashing through hedges, leaping ditches, and thundering over fields, until he ran out of breath, felt worn out, and had to slow to a comfortable walk. Once he had got his wind back and could think clearly, he began to giggle; the giggling turned to laughter, and he laughed so hard that he had to sit down beneath a hedge. “Ho, ho!” he exclaimed, delirious with admiration for himself. “Toad strikes again! Toad, as always, comes out ahead! Who talked them into giving him a ride? Who found a way to sit in front, for the fresh air? Who coaxed them into letting him try the driving? Who dumped the whole lot of them in a horse-pond? And who sailed off merrily and without a scratch through the air, leaving those narrow-minded, mean, timid sightseers lying in the mud, right where they belong? Why, Toad, naturally; clever Toad, marvelous Toad, _good_ Toad!”
Then he burst into song again, and chanted at the top of his voice—

“The motor-car went Poop-poop-poop,
As it raced along the road.
Who was it drove it into a pond?
Brilliant Mr. Toad!
Oh, how clever I am! How clever, how clever, how very clev——”
A faint noise far behind him made him turn his head and look. Oh horror! Oh misery! Oh despair!
Two fields away, a chauffeur in leather gaiters and two big country policemen were running toward him as fast as they could go!

Poor Toad jumped up and dashed off once more, with his heart in his throat. Oh dear!” he gasped between pants, “what an _ass_ I am! What a _vain_ and careless ass! Swaggering again! Bellowing and singing again! Sitting around and blabbing again! Oh dear! Oh dear! Oh dear!”

He glanced back and saw, to his horror, that they were catching up. He ran on desperately, but he kept looking behind him, and each time they had closed in a little more. He did his best, but he was a plump animal with short legs, and still they gained on him. Now he could hear them right at his heels. He stopped paying attention to where he was heading and stumbled on, blind and frantic, staring back over his shoulder at his triumphant enemies—when suddenly the ground vanished beneath his feet, he clutched at empty air, and, splash! he was in deep water over his head. It was fast water, water that swept him along with a force he could not fight; and he understood that in his blind panic he had run straight into the river!

He bobbed up to the surface and tried to catch hold of the reeds and rushes growing along the water’s edge beneath the bank, but the current was so strong that it ripped them out of his hands. “Oh my!” gasped poor Toad. “If I ever steal a motor-car again! If I ever sing another vain song”—and then down he went, and came up breathless and sputtering. Soon he saw that he was drifting toward a big dark hole in the bank, just above his head, and as the current carried him past it he reached up with one paw, caught the edge, and hung on. Then slowly and painfully he hauled himself up out of the water, until at last he could rest his elbows on the edge of the hole. He stayed there for some minutes, puffing and panting, for he was completely worn out.

As he sighed and blew and stared into the dark hole in front of him, something small and bright glinted and twinkled far inside, coming closer. As it drew near, a face slowly formed around it, and it was a familiar face!
Brown and small, with whiskers.
Serious and round, with neat ears and silky fur.
It was the Water Rat!
